nameStory: This jumping spider carries the name 'canadensis' meaning 'from Canada,' reflecting its northern range that extends well into Canadian territory. The genus name Ghelna doesn't have a clear etymological story in common usage, as this is one of the more obscure jumping spider groups that scientists encounter.
description: Ghelna canadensis is a small jumping spider that belongs to the incredibly diverse family of spiders known for their excellent vision and hunting prowess. Like other jumping spiders, it has a compact, robust body and large forward-facing eyes that give it an almost curious, alert expression. These spiders are active hunters that stalk their prey rather than building webs to catch food, making them fascinating to observe in action.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes arranged in a front row, with the middle pair especially prominent and giving the spider an alert, almost mammal-like gaze that seems to follow you

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and sturdy build with a relatively flat, wide cephalothorax (front section) that feels firm to the touch if gently handled

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky jumps followed by sudden stops, often turning to face observers directly with seeming curiosity

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider that could comfortably sit on a dime, with females typically slightly larger than males

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Does not build catching webs, but may leave small silk draglines behind as safety ropes when jumping

habitat: Look for this rare jumping spider in northern New England forests, particularly in areas with mixed coniferous and deciduous trees where it can hunt on bark surfaces and fallen logs. It seems to prefer cooler, shadier microhabitats compared to many other jumping spiders that favor sunny, open areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting season on tree bark and wooden surfaces where prey becomes abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be spotted hunting during warm, sunny days. Mating likely occurs during this season.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, though spiders become less conspicuous as temperatures drop and they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters in protected locations under bark or in leaf litter, remaining dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Despite being called 'canadensis,' this spider has been recorded only once in New England, making any sighting an incredibly rare discovery that could contribute valuable scientific data about its true range and habitat preferences.
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for other small jumping spiders in the region, but the key is looking for that characteristic jumping spider eye arrangement - four large eyes in the front row with the middle pair being especially large and prominent, giving them their signature 'intelligent' appearance.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents one of the more mysterious members of New England's jumping spider fauna, with so few recorded observations that much of its natural history remains unknown to science.
compareHints: Since this is the only Ghelna species recorded in New England, compare it with other small jumping spiders like those in the genus Habronattus or Phidippus. Ghelna canadensis tends to be smaller and less colorful than many other jumping spiders, lacking the bright colors or distinctive markings that make species like the bold jumping spider so recognizable.
